Action Plan:
1) Same-day in-person assessment at a clinic/GP for wheeze/shortness of breath, including a finger pulse oximetry check (oxygen saturation).
2) Obtain an over-the-counter antihistamine en route if possible; if not obtainable, the GP/clinic can prescribe one.
3) Oral steroids may be required depending on in-person assessment results (to be decided after evaluation).
4) Clinician will send a letter to the patient’s GP via the app; patient to present this for the in-person visit (anticipated duration ~10 minutes).
5) Verbal consent from patient has been obtained before using transcription software.

Subjective:
- Reason for visit: Wheezing and shortness of breath.
- History of present illness:
  - Onset: Began ~2 days ago after cleaning with significant dust exposure; started about an hour post-exposure.
  - Course: Getting worse over 2 days; worse at night.
  - Severity/impact: Short of breath; sometimes unable to complete sentences when talking.
  - Associated symptoms: No chest pain with deep breath; no dizziness.
  - Self-care/meds tried: None for this episode; has not used inhaler.
- Past medical history:
  - Childhood asthma; residual exercise-induced symptoms at times.
  - Seasonal hay fever.
  - Prior courses of steroids for asthma (dose/route/frequency not documented).
- Medications:
  - Asthma inhaler at home from a couple of months ago (type/dose/frequency not documented); not used during this episode.
  - No regular antihistamine currently; none at home.
- Social history:
  - Able to drive; clinic/GP is minutes away (exact time not stated).
  - Smoking status not discussed.
- Allergies:
  - No known allergies reported.

Objective:
- Telemedicine consult; no physical examination or vitals obtained.
- Respiratory status: Reported wheeze and dyspnea with speech limitation at times; no objective measures recorded.
- Investigations: None performed during call. Plan for pulse oximetry in clinic/GP.
- Technical: Video signal lost mid-call; audio continued.

Assessment & Plan:
1. Wheezing and shortness of breath after dust exposure:
   - Assessment / likely diagnosis: Acute asthma exacerbation triggered by dust/allergen exposure (High likelihood per DDx).
   - Differential diagnosis:
     - Irritant-induced bronchospasm from dust exposure (Medium likelihood per DDx).
     - Allergic rhinitis with lower-airway involvement (Medium likelihood per DDx).
     - Acute viral bronchitis with wheeze (Low likelihood per DDx).
     - Vocal cord dysfunction/inducible laryngeal obstruction (Low likelihood per DDx).
   - Supporting evidence: Atopic history (hay fever), childhood asthma with residual symptoms, onset ~1 hour after dust exposure, nocturnal worsening, wheeze and dyspnea severe enough to limit speech.
   - Opposing/uncertain: No objective pulmonary measurements obtained during call.
   - Investigations planned: In-person assessment with finger pulse oximetry at clinic/GP; further tests as directed by in-person clinician.
   - Treatment planned:
     - Take an over-the-counter antihistamine now if available; if not, obtain prescription at GP/clinic.
     - Possible course of oral steroids depending on in-person evaluation results.
   - Relevant referrals: Letter sent to patient’s GP via app for expedited in-person consult (anticipated ~10 minutes).

Quality checks:
- Missing expected elements:
  - No vitals (respiratory rate, heart rate, blood pressure, oxygen saturation).
  - No lung exam, peak flow, or spirometry.
  - Medication names/types and doses not documented (inhaler unspecified; prior steroid regimen unspecified).
  - Smoking status not recorded.
  - Immunization history not discussed.
- Internal conflicts between transcript and DDx: None noted.
- Transcript quality: Some audio gaps and inaudible segments; video connection lost mid-call, limiting assessment.
